description: I'm James Chimdindu... This will be my third time participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge, coming out as a Global Nominee in 2025. I am majorly a Product/UI/UX Designer but also a multipotentialite. Find out more about me on my website: https://jameschimdindu.com.
summary:
Earth Jukebox lets you hear NASA's pictures of Earth. A voice guide called Juke talks with you, plays the data as music and tells you what each sound means. You can use it with your eyes closed.

NASA's Earth Information Center shows our planet as colour maps. If you cannot see well, a colour map tells you nothing. Earth Jukebox reads six of those maps back into numbers and plays them. A higher note means a higher value. Places to the west sound in your left ear, places to the east in your right. Ask Juke for any city, play two places at once, or hear how a place changed since last year.

Every note comes from a real value. Our pipeline decodes NASA's frames every day and checks them against the data behind each picture. Sea surface temperature, for example, is on average 0.20 °C from the satellite record. Juke only says numbers that the data gives it.
details:
What it does
Earth Jukebox plays NASA Earth Information Center data as sound. Open https://heartheearth.vercel.app, press Start talking (or Type instead), and Juke, a voice guide, greets you at your own place. Choose one of six records: sea surface temperature, its anomaly, near-surface air temperature, polar sea ice, ocean plankton or active fires. Juke first plays a short key: the usual note for this place, a higher note and a drum. Then the track plays, one note per day for the sea and sea ice, per week for plankton and fires, and per 6 hours for air. After the track, Juke says what you heard, with the real number behind the note.

Ask how a place changed since last year, and Juke plays the same day one year apart, the older day in your left ear and the newer day in your right. You can also hear today's note, the highest and lowest moments at a place, or two places at once. A sound postcard saves what you hear as a WAV file, and a link opens the same place and record for someone else.

Why it matters
NASA shows Earth data as colour maps. If you cannot see well, a colour map tells you nothing. Earth Jukebox gives you the same data as sound and speech, so you can explore it with your eyes closed.

Accessibility
Audio comes first. You can use the whole app without looking at the screen. You can talk or type. Every action has a keyboard shortcut, and every question Juke asks also has buttons for its answers. Captions and a full transcript show what Juke says. The app works with a screen reader and follows the reduced motion setting. The accent colour follows the data, and the app lifts it until it has 4.5:1 contrast with the background. The layout is the same on a phone and a desktop.

Make it yours
The globe is drawn in lines by default. Choose Realistic to see NASA's own picture of the record wrapped around the globe, or Realistic with depth to see that picture raised where it is brighter. The Options menu also lets you choose the instrument (strings, piano, marimba, flute, glass bells, synth pad, or Surprise me for a new one each track) and one of four voices for Juke. You can also change the layout, the pin on your place, and how fast the globe spins. Search for any place, or drag the globe.

How it works
NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio publishes each record as frames. Our Python pipeline matches every pixel to the record's colour bar and keeps one value per 1-degree cell. A daily job decodes NASA's newest frames and publishes them. The web app turns each value into pitch with the Web Audio API and places it in 3D sound, west on your left and east on your right. Juke is an ElevenLabs voice agent with Claude as its language model. It controls the app through 20 tools and only says numbers that those tools return.

How we know the notes are right
A sonification can sound good and still be wrong, so we check each record against the data that NASA's picture was made from. Sea surface temperature is on average 0.20 °C from the satellite record (JPL MUR SST), and its anomaly 0.17 °C. Air temperature is 0.7 °C from NASA's GEOS-FP model. Its last hours are a forecast, and Juke says so. Sea ice gives the same answer (ice or no ice) as the satellite record in 94% of checks. Plankton has a median error of about 14% against NOAA's satellite chlorophyll. Where NASA's picture shows fire, NASA's FIRMS detections agree in 86% of the squares.

Tools
JavaScript with three.js and the Web Audio API, in one HTML file. Python with NumPy, SciPy, Pillow and OpenEXR for the pipeline. ElevenLabs Agents with Anthropic Claude for the voice. GitHub Actions for the daily update. Vercel for hosting.

Use of AI
Juke's voice is AI-generated (ElevenLabs), and Juke's words come from Claude. Claude also helped write the code, the data pipeline and the text.
